skill.description: Guides Go database development with parameterized queries, struct scanning, transactions, connection pools, and tests using database/sql, sqlx, or pgx. Excludes schema creation and migration SQL generation.

security_audit.summary: All 102 static findings are false positives involving Go syntax, database examples, documentation links, or evaluation text. No evidence found of malicious execution, credential exfiltration, or audit-directed prompt injection. One semantic concern discourages row-level security without distinguishing existing authorization requirements.

remediation.issue: SKILL.md discourages row-level security alongside convenience features, without preserving database authorization requirements.
remediation.suggestion: Remove the blanket prohibition on row-level security. Preserve existing tenant policies and require security review before changing authorization enforcement.

semantic_findings.title: Blanket Guidance Discourages Row-Level Security
semantic_findings.description: The skill says, "Do not rely on triggers, views, materialized views, stored procedures, or row-level security in application code". Discouraging row-level security without preserving authorization requirements can weaken tenant isolation when developers move enforcement exclusively into application queries.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The prose explicitly groups row-level security with features to avoid and provides no authorization-preservation exception. Actual exposure depends on the application's existing security architecture.

content.user_title: Write and Review Go Database Code
content.value_statement: Go database code can hide query vulnerabilities, connection leaks, and concurrency errors. This skill guides explicit SQL access, transaction handling, performance reviews, and database testing.
actual_capabilities: Guide parameterized SQL, dynamic IN clauses, placeholder rebinding, and allowlisted sort columns.
Explain sqlx and pgx struct scanning, nullable fields, and JSON marshaling choices.
Review context propagation, missing-row handling, row cleanup, and iteration errors.
Provide transaction patterns, isolation choices, and SELECT FOR UPDATE locking guidance.
Suggest connection pool settings, bounded batches, cursor pagination, and index investigations.
Outline repository mocks, sqlmock expectations, build-tagged integration tests, and PostgreSQL test containers.
limitations: Does not generate database schemas or migration SQL; those require dedicated tooling and human review.
Prefers sqlx or pgx and discourages ORMs, so it may conflict with established project conventions.
Examples require project integration and current library API checks; they are not guaranteed to compile unchanged.
Not a complete authorization design guide; its blanket advice against row-level security needs security review.

use_cases.title: Implement Repository Functions
use_cases.description: Develop parameterized queries, nullable result mappings, and explicit not-found behavior for an existing database.

use_cases.title: Review Database Reliability
use_cases.description: Inspect transaction boundaries, connection leaks, pool settings, and batching choices before deployment.

use_cases.title: Plan Database Test Coverage
use_cases.description: Separate service mocks from real SQL integration tests using build tags, transaction rollback, and disposable PostgreSQL containers.

prompt_templates.title: Beginner: Add a User Lookup
prompt_templates.prompt: Using my existing sqlx setup, write a context-aware user lookup by email. Bind parameters, select explicit columns, and handle missing rows without changing schemas.
prompt_templates.scenario: Add a repository method to an existing Go application.

prompt_templates.title: Intermediate: Review Query Safety
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this Go repository for SQL interpolation, missing context, row leaks, and ignored errors. Follow existing conventions and explain each proposed change.
prompt_templates.scenario: Review existing database access code before merging.

prompt_templates.title: Advanced: Protect Concurrent Writes
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this inventory update for concurrency risks. Propose transaction boundaries, row locks, isolation, and retry handling while preserving authorization checks and existing database policies.
prompt_templates.scenario: Improve consistency in a concurrent write workflow.

prompt_templates.title: Expert: Plan Performance and Integration Tests
prompt_templates.prompt: Assess this bulk-import repository using supplied workload measurements. Propose bounded batches, pool settings, and disposable integration tests; do not run production queries or DDL.
prompt_templates.scenario: Prepare a measured performance improvement with repeatable tests.

output_examples.input: Review a lookup that concatenates an email into SQL and returns raw database errors.
output: Replace email interpolation with a bound parameter appropriate for the database driver.
Use the context-aware query method and distinguish missing rows from connection or query failures.
Return a domain-level not-found result and wrap other errors with operation context.

output_examples.input: Plan tests for a repository that creates and retrieves users.
output: Use repository mocks to exercise service behavior without a database.
Verify SQL behavior against a disposable PostgreSQL database under an integration build tag.
Run each repository test inside a transaction and roll it back during teardown.
Cover missing records, nullable fields, constraints, and transaction behavior without using production data.

output_examples.input: Suggest improvements for an import that inserts records individually.
output: Start with bounded batches and adjust their size using row size and workload measurements.
Consider pgx COPY for PostgreSQL bulk inserts when it fits the existing project.
Measure connection pool waits and query behavior before proposing configuration changes.
Present index changes for human review rather than executing schema changes.

best_practices: Provide the database engine, library version, existing schema, and repository conventions before requesting code.
Use disposable test databases, least-privilege credentials, and human review for production performance changes.
Preserve tenant authorization and existing row-level security policies when applying query or architecture recommendations.
anti_patterns: Concatenating untrusted values or unchecked column names into SQL.
Running integration tests against production databases or applying suggested DDL automatically.
Removing authorization policies to follow blanket preferences for application-side SQL.

faq.question: Which AI tools can use this skill?
faq.answer: The skill targets Codex and Claude Code. It provides instructions and reference examples rather than a standalone database application.

faq.question: Which database libraries does it cover?
faq.answer: It covers database/sql, sqlx, and pgx for PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, and SQLite workflows. PostgreSQL-specific examples receive additional attention.

faq.question: Can it generate schemas or migrations?
faq.answer: No. It directs schema design and migration SQL to dedicated tooling and human review.

faq.question: Does it support ORM-based projects?
faq.answer: Its guidance favors explicit SQL through sqlx or pgx and discourages ORMs. Review compatibility with your project's established architecture before applying recommendations.

faq.question: Can the examples run unchanged?
faq.answer: Not reliably. Adapt imports, interfaces, fixtures, and library calls to your project, then compile and test the result.

faq.question: Should I remove existing row-level security?
faq.answer: No. Preserve existing authorization controls and tenant policies. Treat the skill's blanket advice against row-level security as requiring security review.
